source.text: כֹּ֚ה אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה רֵ֖ד בֵּֽית־מֶ֣לֶךְ יְהוּדָ֑ה וְדִבַּרְתָּ֣ שָׁ֔ם אֶת־הַדָּבָ֖ר הַזֶּֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: Thus says Yahweh: go down [to the] house of [the] king of Judah, and you will speak there the word this,

en.L: Thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}: "Go down to the house of the king of Judah, and speak there this word,
en.B: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} says this: "Go down to the palace of Judah's king and speak this message there.
en.R: This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says: "Go down to the palace where the king of Judah lives, and give this message there.

decisions.choice: God speaks to Jeremiah, sending him with a message to the king; the message runs from verse 2 to verse 5
decisions.reason: Verses 1-5 are a short prose sermon like 7:1-15 and 17:19-27. A collection of oracles about the kings of Judah follows from verse 6: about the palace (6-9), Shallum (10-12), Jehoiakim (13-19), Jerusalem (20-23) and Coniah (24-30). It continues the word to the royal house begun in 21:11-14, which also calls the king to do justice.

decisions.choice: go down: from the temple, which stood on higher ground, to the palace below it
decisions.reason: The royal palace stood just south of the temple and lower on the same hill, so a prophet coming from the temple court went down to it (compare 26:10 and 36:12, where officials go up from the palace to the temple and down again).

decisions.choice: the palace (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: "The house of the king" is the royal palace; Balanced and Readable say so. Literal keeps "house", which in verse 5 and later in the chapter also hints at the royal family.

decisions.choice: Thus says the LORD: (L); The LORD says this: (B); This is what the LORD says: (R)
decisions.reason: The wording set for this formula in Isaiah and Jeremiah. Because God's instruction to Jeremiah is prose and contains the words he is to say, it is quoted as prose speech, as in 19:1-13.

source.text: וְאָֽמַרְתָּ֙ שְׁמַ֣ע דְּבַר־יְהוָ֔ה מֶ֣לֶךְ יְהוּדָ֔ה הַיֹּשֵׁ֖ב עַל־כִּסֵּ֣א דָוִ֑ד אַתָּ֤ה וַעֲבָדֶ֨יךָ֙ וְעַמְּךָ֔ הַבָּאִ֖ים בַּשְּׁעָרִ֥ים הָאֵֽלֶּה׃ס

records.literal_gloss: and you will say: Hear [the] word of Yahweh, king of Judah, the [one] sitting on [the] throne of David, you and your servants and your people, the [ones] entering through the gates these.

en.L: and say, 'Hear the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, king of Judah, who sits on the throne of David, you and your servants and your people who enter through these gates.
en.B: Say: 'Hear the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, king of Judah, you who sit on David's throne, you and your officials and your people who come in through these gates.
en.R: Say: 'King of Judah, you who rule from David's throne, listen to this message from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. Listen, you and your officials and all your people who come in through these gates.

decisions.choice: who sits on the throne of David: the reigning king, as heir of the promise to David
decisions.reason: The king is named by his place in David's line, which recalls God's promise that David's house and throne would last (2 Samuel 7:16). The whole chapter turns on whether David's heirs will keep that throne (verses 4 and 30).

decisions.choice: your servants: the king's officials at court
decisions.reason: Here the word means the men who served the king in government, not slaves.

decisions.choice: these gates: the gates of the palace
decisions.reason: The king, his court and the people who had business there came and went through the palace gates. Verse 4 names them "the gates of this house".

decisions.choice: officials (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: As Isaiah and the earlier books do for a king's court, Literal keeps "servants" and Balanced and Readable say "officials".

source.text: כֹּ֣ה׀אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֗ה עֲשׂ֤וּ מִשְׁפָּט֙ וּצְדָקָ֔ה וְהַצִּ֥ילוּ גָז֖וּל מִיַּ֣ד עָשׁ֑וֹק וְגֵר֩ יָת֨וֹם וְאַלְמָנָ֤ה אַל־תֹּנוּ֙ אַל־תַּחְמֹ֔סוּ וְדָ֣ם נָקִ֔י אַֽל־תִּשְׁפְּכ֖וּ בַּמָּק֥וֹם הַזֶּֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: Thus says Yahweh: do justice and righteousness, and deliver [the] robbed from [the] hand of [the] oppressor, and [the] sojourner, [the] fatherless and [the] widow do not wrong, do not treat violently, and blood innocent do not shed in the place this.

en.L: Thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}: Do justice and righteousness, and rescue the robbed from the hand of the oppressor. Do not wrong the sojourner, the fatherless, or the widow; do no violence; and do not shed innocent blood in this place.
en.B: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} says this: Practice justice and righteousness. Rescue anyone who has been robbed from the power of the oppressor. Do not mistreat the outsider, the orphan or the widow, do not use violence against them, and do not shed innocent blood in this place.
en.R: This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says: Do what is fair and right. Rescue people who have been robbed from those who oppress them. Do not mistreat or harm strangers, orphans or widows, and do not kill innocent people in this place.

decisions.choice: do justice and righteousness: rule and act fairly, giving every person what is right
decisions.reason: The two words are often paired (verse 15; 2 Samuel 8:15; Isaiah 9:6) for fair judgment together with right dealing. Together they describe the king's first duty: to see that the weak get their rights.

decisions.choice: the sojourner, the fatherless and the widow: people with no family or land to protect them
decisions.reason: A sojourner was a person from elsewhere living among Israel without the rights of a landholder; orphans and widows had lost the men who would defend them in court. The Law names these three together as those God himself protects (Deuteronomy 10:18; 24:17; Exodus 22:20-23), and Jeremiah's temple sermon repeats the same charge (7:6).

decisions.choice: shed innocent blood: put innocent people to death
decisions.reason: The phrase covers murder and also judicial killing of the innocent. Jehoiakim is charged with it in verse 17 (compare 26:20-23, the killing of the prophet Uriah).

decisions.choice: what is fair and right (Readable)
decisions.reason: Readable puts the pair "justice and righteousness" in everyday words; the same pair returns in verse 15.

decisions.choice: outsider (Balanced); strangers (Readable)
decisions.reason: The wording set for this word (sojourner, outsider, stranger) since Leviticus; "foreigner" is kept for another Hebrew word.

source.text: כִּ֤י אִם־עָשׂוֹ֙ תַּֽעֲשׂ֔וּ אֶת־הַדָּבָ֖ר הַזֶּ֑ה וּבָ֣אוּ בְשַׁעֲרֵ֣י הַבַּ֣יִת הַזֶּ֡ה מְלָכִים֩ יֹשְׁבִ֨ים לְדָוִ֜ד עַל־כִּסְא֗וֹ רֹֽכְבִים֙ בָּרֶ֣כֶב וּבַסּוּסִ֔ים ה֥וּא וַעֲבָדָ֖יו וְעַמּֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: For if doing you do the word this, then will enter through [the] gates of the house this kings sitting for David on his throne, riding in chariot and on horses, he and his servants and his people.

en.L: For if you indeed do this word, then there will enter through the gates of this house kings who sit for David on his throne, riding in chariots and on horses, he and his servants and his people.
en.B: For if you are careful to do what this word commands, then kings who sit on David's throne will come in through the gates of this palace, riding in chariots and on horses, each with his officials and his people.
en.R: If you really obey this command, kings from David's family will go on ruling from his throne. They will ride in chariots and on horses through the gates of this palace, together with their officials and their people.

decisions.choice: if you indeed do: the doubled verb stresses real, careful obedience
decisions.reason: Hebrew repeats the verb to make it emphatic: doing it in earnest, not in part.

decisions.choice: kings sitting for David on his throne: David's heirs, reigning in his place one after another
decisions.reason: "For David" means as David's successors. The promise is that the dynasty will go on, as in 17:25, where the same picture of kings riding through the gates is given as a reward for keeping the sabbath.

decisions.choice: his servants: the plural read aloud
decisions.reason: The written consonants could be read as "his servant"; the form read aloud is "his servants", which matches verse 2. The meaning is the same.

decisions.choice: kings from David's family will go on ruling
decisions.reason: Readable spells out that the promise is for David's line to continue.

source.text: וְאִם֙ לֹ֣א תִשְׁמְע֔וּ אֶת־הַדְּבָרִ֖ים הָאֵ֑לֶּה בִּ֤י נִשְׁבַּ֨עְתִּי֙ נְאֻם־יְהוָ֔ה כִּי־לְחָרְבָּ֥ה יִֽהְיֶ֖ה הַבַּ֥יִת הַזֶּֽה׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And if not you will hear the words these, by myself I swear, declares Yahweh, that a ruin will become the house this.

en.L: But if you will not hear these words, by {{deity_pronoun:myself|Myself}} I swear, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, that this house will become a ruin.'"
en.B: But if you will not listen to these words, I swear by {{deity_pronoun:myself|Myself}}, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, that this palace will become a ruin.'"
en.R: But if you will not obey these words, I swear by {{deity_pronoun:myself|Myself}}, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, that this palace will be left in ruins.'"

decisions.choice: by myself I swear: God binds himself by an oath on his own life and name
decisions.reason: There is no one greater for God to swear by, so he swears by himself (Genesis 22:16; Isaiah 45:23). The oath makes the warning certain.

decisions.choice: this house: the palace, with the royal family it stands for
decisions.reason: The house that becomes a ruin is the palace building (verse 6), but "house" also means a dynasty (2 Samuel 7:11-16), and the chapter goes on to say that the line itself will lose the throne (verse 30).

decisions.choice: declares the LORD (L, B); says the LORD (R)
decisions.reason: The wording set for this formula in Isaiah and Jeremiah. The quotation that began in verse 1 closes here.

source.text: כִּֽי־כֹ֣ה׀אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֗ה עַל־בֵּית֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ יְהוּדָ֔ה גִּלְעָ֥ד אַתָּ֛ה לִ֖י רֹ֣אשׁ הַלְּבָנ֑וֹן אִם־לֹ֤א אֲשִֽׁיתְךָ֙ מִדְבָּ֔ר עָרִ֖ים לֹ֥א נוֹשָֽׁבוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: For thus says Yahweh concerning [the] house of [the] king of Judah: Gilead [are] you to me, [the] head of the Lebanon; if not I will make you a wilderness, cities not inhabited.

en.L: For thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} concerning the house of the king of Judah: \q You [are] Gilead to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, the summit of Lebanon; \q yet surely I will make you a wilderness, \q cities not inhabited.
en.B: For {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says this about the palace of the king of Judah: \q To {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} you are like Gilead, like the heights of Lebanon, \q but I will surely make you a wilderness, \q like towns where no one lives.
en.R: This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says about the palace of the king of Judah: \q To {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} you are as fine as the forests of Gilead, as splendid as the top of the Lebanon mountains. \q But I will turn you into a desert, \q like towns where no one lives.

decisions.choice: Gilead, the summit of Lebanon: places famous for their forests, here a picture of the cedar-built palace
decisions.reason: Gilead east of the Jordan and the Lebanon mountains in the north were known for tall trees, and Lebanon above all for cedar. Solomon's great hall built of cedar was called "the House of the Forest of Lebanon" (1 Kings 7:2). The palace is as grand and green as those forests, and as easily felled (verse 7).

decisions.choice: if not I will make you: a form of oath, meaning "I will surely make you"
decisions.reason: The words "if I do not ..." stand for an oath with its curse left unspoken; they mean the opposite of what they seem to say: "I will certainly do it".

decisions.choice: you: the palace, and the royal house it stands for
decisions.reason: God speaks to the palace as a person. The "cities" that are not inhabited compare its fate to towns left empty after war (4:7).

decisions.choice: like Gilead, like the peak (Balanced); as fine as the forests of Gilead (Readable)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew sets the names side by side as a picture; Balanced adds "like" and Readable says what the picture compares.

source.text: וְקִדַּשְׁתִּ֥י עָלֶ֛יךָ מַשְׁחִתִ֖ים אִ֣ישׁ וְכֵלָ֑יו וְכָֽרְתוּ֙ מִבְחַ֣ר אֲרָזֶ֔יךָ וְהִפִּ֖ילוּ עַל־הָאֵֽשׁ׃

records.literal_gloss: And I will consecrate against you destroyers, a man and his weapons, and they will cut down [the] choicest of your cedars and will cast [them] on the fire.

en.L: And I will consecrate destroyers against you, each with his weapons, \q and they will cut down the choicest of your cedars \q and throw [them] into the fire.
en.B: I will appoint destroyers against you, each with his weapons. \q They will cut down your finest cedars \q and throw them into the fire.
en.R: I will send destroyers against you, each one armed. \q They will cut down your finest cedar beams \q and throw them into the fire.

decisions.choice: consecrate: set apart and make ready for a holy war
decisions.reason: The verb means to make holy; used of soldiers it means to prepare them for a war fought at God's command (6:4; 51:27-28; Joel 4:9). God is the one who musters the enemy against his own city.

decisions.choice: your choicest cedars: the cedar pillars and beams of the palace
decisions.reason: The picture of the forest from verse 6 continues: the cedars cut down are the palace timbers (1 Kings 7:2-3). Jerusalem's palace was burned in 587 BC (39:8; 52:13).

decisions.choice: appoint (Balanced); send (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the sense of the verb rather than "consecrate", which Literal keeps.

decisions.choice: cedar beams
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear that the cedars are the timbers of the building.

source.text: וְעָֽבְרוּ֙ גּוֹיִ֣ם רַבִּ֔ים עַ֖ל הָעִ֣יר הַזֹּ֑את וְאָֽמְרוּ֙ אִ֣ישׁ אֶל־רֵעֵ֔הוּ עַל־מֶ֨ה עָשָׂ֤ה יְהוָה֙ כָּ֔כָה לָעִ֥יר הַגְּדוֹלָ֖ה הַזֹּֽאת׃

records.literal_gloss: And will pass many nations by the city this, and they will say each to his neighbor: For what has done Yahweh thus to the city great this?

en.L: And many nations will pass by this city, and they will say each to his neighbor, "Why has {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} done thus to this great city?"
en.B: People of many nations will pass by this city and say to one another, "Why has {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} treated this great city like this?"
en.R: People from many nations will walk past this city. They will ask one another, "Why did {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} do this to such a great city?"

decisions.choice: the question of the passing nations: the curse of the covenant foretold in the Law and at the temple's dedication
decisions.reason: Deuteronomy 29:23-25 and 1 Kings 9:8-9 give the same question and answer: people seeing the ruined land or house ask why the LORD did this, and are told that Israel forsook his covenant.

decisions.choice: people of many nations
decisions.reason: "Nations" here means people from those nations who travel past; Balanced and Readable say so.

source.text: וְאָ֣מְר֔וּ עַ֚ל אֲשֶׁ֣ר עָֽזְב֔וּ אֶת־בְּרִ֥ית יְהוָ֖ה אֱלֹֽהֵיהֶ֑ם וַיִּֽשְׁתַּחֲו֛וּ לֵאלֹהִ֥ים אֲחֵרִ֖ים וַיַּעַבְדֽוּם׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And they will say: Because they forsook [the] covenant of Yahweh their God and they bowed down to other gods and served them.

en.L: And they will say, "Because they forsook the covenant of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} their God and bowed down to other gods and served them."
en.B: And the answer will be, "Because they abandoned the covenant of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} their God and worshiped other gods and served them."
en.R: And others will answer, "It is because the people abandoned the covenant they had with {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} their God. They worshiped other gods and served them."

decisions.choice: they forsook the covenant: the ruin comes from breaking the covenant, not from the LORD's weakness
decisions.reason: The nations' answer says that the city fell because its people left the LORD for other gods, the first of the covenant's commands (Exodus 20:3-5), not because their God could not protect it.

decisions.choice: bowed down: worshiped
decisions.reason: As in 7:2, the verb of bowing low names the act of worship.

decisions.choice: the answer will be (Balanced); others will answer (Readable)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says only "they will say"; the speakers answer the question of verse 8, and Balanced and Readable make that plain.

source.text: אַל־תִּבְכּ֣וּ לְמֵ֔ת וְאַל־תָּנֻ֖דוּ ל֑וֹ בְּכ֤וּ בָכוֹ֙ לַֽהֹלֵ֔ךְ כִּ֣י לֹ֤א יָשׁוּב֙ ע֔וֹד וְרָאָ֖ה אֶת־אֶ֥רֶץ מוֹלַדְתּֽוֹ׃ס

records.literal_gloss: Do not weep for [the] dead and do not show grief for him; weep weeping for [the one] going, for not he will return again and see [the] land of his kindred.

en.L: Do not weep for the dead, \q and do not grieve for him; \q weep bitterly for the one who goes away, \q for he will not return again \q and see the land of his birth.
en.B: Do not weep for the one who is dead; \q do not mourn for him. \q Weep and keep weeping for the one who is going away, \q because he will never return \q or see his homeland again.
en.R: Do not cry for the king who has died \q or mourn for him. \q Instead, cry hard for the king who is being taken away, \q because he will never come back \q to see his homeland again.

decisions.choice: the dead: King Josiah; the one going away: his son Shallum, taken to Egypt
decisions.reason: Josiah was killed at Megiddo by Pharaoh Neco in 609 BC and was deeply mourned (2 Kings 23:29-30; 2 Chronicles 35:24-25). Three months later Neco removed his son and successor and took him to Egypt (2 Kings 23:31-34). Verse 11 names him. The fate of the living exile is worse than the death of the good king.

decisions.choice: weep weeping: weep bitterly, without stopping
decisions.reason: The verb is doubled for emphasis, the opposite of the two commands not to weep that come before it.

decisions.choice: show grief: shake the head or rock the body in sympathy, as mourners did
decisions.reason: The verb means to move to and fro; it is used for nodding or shaking the head in grief and comfort (15:5; 16:5; Job 2:11).

decisions.choice: the king who has died; the king who is being taken away
decisions.reason: Readable names both as kings, which verses 11-12 make clear; it does not name them in the verse itself.

source.text: כִּ֣י כֹ֣ה אָֽמַר־יְ֠הוָה אֶל־שַׁלֻּ֨ם בֶּן־יֹאשִׁיָּ֜הוּ מֶ֣לֶךְ יְהוּדָ֗ה הַמֹּלֵךְ֙ תַּ֚חַת יֹאשִׁיָּ֣הוּ אָבִ֔יו אֲשֶׁ֥ר יָצָ֖א מִן־הַמָּק֣וֹם הַזֶּ֑ה לֹֽא־יָשׁ֥וּב שָׁ֖ם עֽוֹד׃

records.literal_gloss: For thus says Yahweh to Shallum son of Josiah king of Judah, the [one] reigning in place of Josiah his father, who went out from the place this: Not he will return there again.

en.L: For thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} concerning Shallum son of Josiah, king of Judah, who reigned in place of Josiah his father, who went out from this place: He will not return here again.
en.B: For {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says this about Shallum son of Josiah, king of Judah, who became king in place of his father Josiah and has gone away from this place: He will never come back here.
en.R: This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says about Shallum son of Josiah, who became king of Judah after his father Josiah and has been taken away from this place: He will never come back here.

decisions.choice: Shallum son of Josiah: the king called Jehoahaz in 2 Kings 23:30-34
decisions.reason: Shallum is listed as a son of Josiah in 1 Chronicles 3:15. The king who reigned three months after Josiah and was taken to Egypt is called Jehoahaz in 2 Kings 23:30-34 and 2 Chronicles 36:1-4; Shallum was probably his personal name and Jehoahaz the name he took as king. Each passage keeps the name its Hebrew uses.

decisions.choice: to Shallum: about Shallum
decisions.reason: The preposition can mean "to" or "concerning"; Shallum is spoken of, not spoken to, so it means "concerning" here, as in verse 18.

decisions.choice: went out: was taken away as a prisoner
decisions.reason: He did not leave by choice; Neco took him away (2 Kings 23:33-34). Verse 12 says he was taken into exile.

decisions.choice: has been taken away
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly that he was forced to go.

source.text: כִּ֗י בִּמְק֛וֹם אֲשֶׁר־הִגְל֥וּ אֹת֖וֹ שָׁ֣ם יָמ֑וּת וְאֶת־הָאָ֥רֶץ הַזֹּ֖את לֹֽא־יִרְאֶ֥ה עֽוֹד׃ס

records.literal_gloss: For in [the] place where they exiled him, there he will die, and the land this not he will see again.

en.L: For in the place where they have exiled him, there he will die, and this land he will not see again.
en.B: He will die in the place where they have taken him as a captive, and he will never see this land again.
en.R: He will die in the country where they took him as a prisoner. He will never see this land again.

decisions.choice: the place where they exiled him: Egypt, where Jehoahaz died
decisions.reason: 2 Kings 23:34 records that he went to Egypt and died there, as this word says.

decisions.choice: no "for" at the start (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: The opening word here marks a contrast with "he will not return" ("but", "instead"); Balanced and Readable leave it unspoken and let the sentences follow one another.

source.text: ה֣וֹי בֹּנֶ֤ה בֵיתוֹ֙ בְּֽלֹא־צֶ֔דֶק וַעֲלִיּוֹתָ֖יו בְּלֹ֣א מִשְׁפָּ֑ט בְּרֵעֵ֨הוּ֙ יַעֲבֹ֣ד חִנָּ֔ם וּפֹעֲל֖וֹ לֹ֥א יִתֶּן־לֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: Woe, [the one] building his house by not righteousness and his upper rooms by not justice; by his neighbor he works for nothing, and his wages not he gives to him.

en.L: Woe, he who builds his house without righteousness \q and his upper rooms without justice, \q who makes his neighbor work for nothing \q and does not give him his wages,
en.B: Woe to the man who builds his palace without righteousness \q and his upper rooms without justice, \q who makes his fellow citizens work for nothing \q and does not pay them their wages.
en.R: How terrible it will be for the king who builds his palace by doing wrong \q and adds rooms upstairs by cheating people. \q He makes his own people work for nothing \q and does not pay them for their work.

decisions.choice: the builder: King Jehoiakim, Josiah's son, named in verse 18
decisions.reason: After Neco removed Jehoahaz, he made his brother Eliakim king and renamed him Jehoiakim (2 Kings 23:34-35). Jehoiakim paid Egypt heavy tribute taxed from the people, and this oracle charges him with building himself a new palace with forced, unpaid labor.

decisions.choice: by his neighbor he works for nothing: he makes his fellow Israelites work for him without pay
decisions.reason: "Neighbor" is a fellow member of the people. The Law forbids holding back a worker's wages even overnight (Leviticus 19:13; Deuteronomy 24:14-15), and Samuel had warned that kings would put the people to work for themselves (1 Samuel 8:11-17).

decisions.choice: without righteousness, without justice: by wrongdoing, not merely without virtue
decisions.reason: "By not-righteousness" means by unjust means: the house is built out of wrongs done to others, the very opposite of the command in verse 3.

decisions.choice: Woe, ... (L); Woe to ... (B); How terrible it will be for ... (R)
decisions.reason: The wording set for this cry in Isaiah, used for Jeremiah as well.

decisions.choice: by doing wrong; by cheating people
decisions.reason: Readable says what "without righteousness" and "without justice" mean here.

source.text: הָאֹמֵ֗ר אֶבְנֶה־לִּי֙ בֵּ֣ית מִדּ֔וֹת וַעֲלִיּ֖וֹת מְרֻוָּחִ֑ים וְקָ֤רַֽע לוֹ֙ חַלּוֹנָ֔י וְסָפ֣וּן בָּאָ֔רֶז וּמָשׁ֖וֹחַ בַּשָּׁשַֽׁר׃

records.literal_gloss: The [one] saying: I will build for myself a house of dimensions and upper rooms spacious; and he cuts out for himself my windows, and [it is] paneled with cedar and painting with vermilion.

en.L: who says, "I will build myself a house of [great] size, \q and spacious upper rooms," \q and cuts out windows for it, \q paneling [it] with cedar and painting [it] with vermilion.
en.B: He says, "I will build myself a huge palace \q with spacious upper rooms." \q He cuts windows into it, \q panels it with cedar and paints it with vermilion.
en.R: He says, "I will build myself a huge palace \q with large rooms upstairs." \q He puts in windows, \q covers the walls with cedar and paints them bright red.

decisions.choice: windows for it: the ending of the word read as part of the plural, not as "my"
decisions.reason: As written, the word looks like "my windows". That would make the king still speaking, which fits poorly after "he cuts out". The ending is probably a form of the plural, or a slip for "his windows"; either way the sense is that he cuts windows in the house.

decisions.choice: cedar and vermilion: costly cedar paneling and bright red paint
decisions.reason: Cedar was imported from Lebanon and used in palaces and the temple (1 Kings 6:9; 7:2-3). Vermilion was a red pigment, a luxury colour (Ezekiel 23:14).

decisions.choice: a house of dimensions, spacious upper rooms: a large palace with airy rooms on the upper floor
decisions.reason: "A house of measures" means one of great size; "spacious" describes rooms open to the air, the cool upper rooms of a fine house.

decisions.choice: bright red (Readable)
decisions.reason: Readable names the colour instead of the pigment.

source.text: הֲתִֽמְלֹ֔ךְ כִּ֥י אַתָּ֖ה מְתַחֲרֶ֣ה בָאָ֑רֶז אָבִ֜יךָ הֲל֧וֹא אָכַ֣ל וְשָׁתָ֗ה וְעָשָׂ֤ה מִשְׁפָּט֙ וּצְדָקָ֔ה אָ֖ז ט֥וֹב לֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: Will you reign because you [are] competing in cedar? Your father, did not he eat and drink and do justice and righteousness? Then [it was] good for him.

en.L: Do you reign because you compete in cedar? \q Your father, did he not eat and drink \q and do justice and righteousness? \q Then [it was] well with him.
en.B: Does it make you a king to outdo others in cedar? \q Did not your father eat and drink \q and also do justice and righteousness? \q Then all went well with him.
en.R: Does having more cedar than anyone else make you a real king? \q Your father had food and drink, \q and he did what was fair and right, \q and so things went well for him.

decisions.choice: will you reign because you compete in cedar: does trying to outdo others in grand cedar buildings make a man a king?
decisions.reason: The verb "compete" is the one used in 12:5 for racing against horses. The question mocks a king who thinks splendor proves his kingship.

decisions.choice: your father ate and drank and did justice: Josiah enjoyed an ordinary, full life and still ruled justly, and that is what made him a true king
alternatives: he was content with plain food and drink, not luxury
decisions.reason: "Eat and drink" means living well and in peace (1 Kings 4:20). Josiah had what a king needs and did not need palaces built by injustice; his kingship showed in his justice. Some take the words to mean that he was content with simple food and drink instead of luxury; either way the stress falls on the justice he did.

decisions.choice: then it was good for him: because of his justice, things went well for him
decisions.reason: The words echo the Law's promise that it will go well for those who do what is right (Deuteronomy 6:18; 12:28). The same phrase returns in verse 16.

decisions.choice: the question about Josiah becomes a statement (Readable)
decisions.reason: The question expects the answer "yes"; Readable gives the answer as a statement.

decisions.choice: what was fair and right
decisions.reason: As in verse 3.

source.text: דָּ֛ן דִּין־עָנִ֥י וְאֶבְי֖וֹן אָ֣ז ט֑וֹב הֲלוֹא־הִ֛יא הַדַּ֥עַת אֹתִ֖י נְאֻם־יְהוָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: He judged [the] cause of [the] poor and needy; then [it was] good. Not [is] that the knowing me? declares Yahweh.

en.L: He judged the cause of the poor and needy; then [it was] well. \q Is not that what it is to know {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}? declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.B: He defended the cause of the poor and the needy, and then all was well. \q Is that not what it means to know {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}? declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.R: He stood up for the rights of poor people and those in need, and everything went well. \q That is what it means to know {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

decisions.choice: judged the cause of the poor and needy: took up their case and saw that they received justice
decisions.reason: To "judge the cause" of someone is to hear their case and decide for them in court; for the poor, who had no one else to plead for them, it meant defending them (5:28; Psalm 72:2-4).

decisions.choice: is not that to know me: to know the LORD is to do justice for the weak, not only to know about him
alternatives: knowing God leads to doing justice (the second is the fruit of the first)
decisions.reason: In Jeremiah, knowing God is a relationship that shows in conduct (9:23; 31:34). Josiah's care for the poor was itself knowledge of God, because it is what God himself does and delights in. Knowing God and doing justice are not two things set side by side here; the one is the form of the other (Hosea 4:1-2; 6:6).

decisions.choice: the question becomes a statement (Readable)
decisions.reason: The question expects "yes", so Readable states the answer.

source.text: כִּ֣י אֵ֤ין עֵינֶ֨יךָ֙ וְלִבְּךָ֔ כִּ֖י אִם־עַל־בִּצְעֶ֑ךָ וְעַ֤ל דַּֽם־הַנָּקִי֙ לִשְׁפּ֔וֹךְ וְעַל־הָעֹ֥שֶׁק וְעַל־הַמְּרוּצָ֖ה לַעֲשֽׂוֹת׃ס

records.literal_gloss: For not [are] your eyes and your heart except on your gain, and on the blood of the innocent to shed [it], and on the oppression and on the extortion to do [them].

en.L: But your eyes and your heart are on nothing \q except your unjust gain, \q and on shedding the blood of the innocent, \q and on doing oppression and extortion.
en.B: But your eyes and your heart are set on nothing \q but dishonest gain, \q on shedding innocent blood, \q and on practicing oppression and extortion.
en.R: But all you care about is getting rich by cheating, \q killing innocent people, \q and crushing people and taking what is theirs.

decisions.choice: your: Jehoiakim, now spoken to directly
decisions.reason: Verses 13-16 spoke about the builder and to him; here the king is addressed and contrasted with his father. Verse 18 names him.

decisions.choice: your gain: profit gained by violence or fraud
decisions.reason: The word means gain cut off unfairly, ill-gotten profit (6:13; 8:10).

decisions.choice: shedding innocent blood: putting to death those who had done nothing worthy of death
decisions.reason: Jeremiah 26:20-23 tells how Jehoiakim had the prophet Uriah hunted down in Egypt and killed. Compare verse 3.

decisions.choice: crushing people and taking what is theirs
decisions.reason: Readable explains "oppression and extortion" in plain words.

source.text: לָכֵ֞ן כֹּֽה־אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֗ה אֶל־יְהוֹיָקִ֤ים בֶּן־יֹאשִׁיָּ֨הוּ֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ יְהוּדָ֔ה לֹא־יִסְפְּד֣וּ ל֔וֹ ה֥וֹי אָחִ֖י וְה֣וֹי אָח֑וֹת לֹא־יִסְפְּד֣וּ ל֔וֹ ה֥וֹי אָד֖וֹן וְה֥וֹי הֹדֹֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: Therefore thus says Yahweh concerning Jehoiakim son of Josiah king of Judah: Not they will lament for him: Alas, my brother, and alas, sister! Not they will lament for him: Alas, lord, and alas, his majesty!

en.L: Therefore thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} concerning Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah: \q They will not lament for him, \q "Alas, my brother!" or "Alas, sister!" \q They will not lament for him, \q "Alas, lord!" or "Alas, his majesty!"
en.B: Therefore {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says this about Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah: \q No one will mourn for him, crying, \q "Alas, my brother! Alas, my sister!" \q No one will mourn for him, crying, \q "Alas, my master! Alas, his majesty!"
en.R: So this is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says about Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah: \q No one will cry at his funeral, \q "How sad, my brother! How sad, my sister!" \q No one will weep for him and say, \q "How sad, our master! How sad for our great king!"

decisions.choice: alas: the cry of mourners at a funeral
decisions.reason: The same word that begins the woe in verse 13 is here the wail of lament over the dead (1 Kings 13:30). The woe pronounced on Jehoiakim takes the place of the mourning he will not receive.

decisions.choice: my brother, sister, lord, his majesty: the set cries of funeral lament
alternatives: the mourners address one another as brother and sister
decisions.reason: Mourners wailed for the dead by calling out to them, "Alas, my brother!" (1 Kings 13:30), and for a king, "Alas, lord!" (34:5). "Sister" may be the women mourners calling to one another, or part of a fixed pair of cries. Jehoiakim will have none of them.

decisions.choice: Alas (Literal and Balanced); How sad (Readable)
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced say "Alas", the wording set for this funeral cry in Jeremiah (as in 34:5); Readable uses words a modern mourner might say. Because this is a cry of grief, it is not given the "Woe to" wording of verse 13.

source.text: קְבוּרַ֥ת חֲמ֖וֹר יִקָּבֵ֑ר סָח֣וֹב וְהַשְׁלֵ֔ךְ מֵהָ֖לְאָה לְשַׁעֲרֵ֥י יְרוּשָׁלִָֽם׃ס

records.literal_gloss: [The] burial of a donkey he will be buried, being dragged and being thrown out beyond to [the] gates of Jerusalem.

en.L: [With] the burial of a donkey he will be buried, \q dragged off and thrown out beyond the gates of Jerusalem.
en.B: He will be buried the way a donkey is buried, \q dragged away and thrown out beyond the gates of Jerusalem.
en.R: He will be buried like a dead donkey. \q His body will be dragged away and thrown outside the gates of Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: the burial of a donkey: no burial at all; the body is dragged away and left like a dead animal
decisions.reason: A dead donkey was hauled out of town and dumped. To be denied burial was a great disgrace (16:4; 36:30, where the same is said of Jehoiakim: his body will be thrown out to the heat by day and the frost by night).

decisions.choice: how Jehoiakim's death came about is not told
decisions.reason: 2 Kings 24:6 says only that he "lay down with his fathers" and his son reigned in his place, which tells of his death but not of a burial. He died in 598 BC as the Babylonian army was coming against Jerusalem. Nothing in the histories describes the fate of his body.

decisions.choice: his body
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear that it is the dead king's body that is dragged away.

source.text: עֲלִ֤י הַלְּבָנוֹן֙ וּֽצְעָ֔קִי וּבַבָּשָׁ֖ן תְּנִ֣י קוֹלֵ֑ךְ וְצַֽעֲקִי֙ מֵֽעֲבָרִ֔ים כִּ֥י נִשְׁבְּר֖וּ כָּל־מְאַהֲבָֽיִךְ׃

records.literal_gloss: Go up [to] the Lebanon and cry out, and in the Bashan give your voice, and cry out from Abarim, for are broken all your lovers.

en.L: Go up to Lebanon and cry out, \q and in Bashan raise your voice; \q cry out from Abarim, \q for all your lovers are broken.
en.B: Climb up to Lebanon and cry out; \q let your voice be heard in Bashan; \q cry out from the Abarim mountains, \q for all your lovers have been crushed.
en.R: People of Jerusalem, go up to Lebanon and scream; \q shout in the land of Bashan; \q cry out from the mountains of Abarim, \q because all your allies have been crushed.

decisions.choice: the one addressed: Jerusalem, pictured as a woman
decisions.reason: The commands are feminine singular. As often in Jeremiah (2:20-25; 4:30), the city is spoken to as a woman, and the address runs to verse 23.

decisions.choice: Lebanon, Bashan, Abarim: high places to the north, the northeast and the southeast, from which a cry would carry far
decisions.reason: Lebanon lies to the north, Bashan east of the Sea of Galilee, and the Abarim range in Moab east of the Dead Sea; Moses viewed the land from it (Numbers 27:12). From every height around the land the city is to wail.

decisions.choice: your lovers: the allies Judah trusted instead of the LORD
decisions.reason: Jeremiah uses "lovers" for the nations Judah courted for help, Egypt and others (2:33-37; 4:30; 30:14), as if a faithless wife ran after other men.

decisions.choice: People of Jerusalem
decisions.reason: Readable names who is spoken to, from verse 23 and the context.

decisions.choice: allies
decisions.reason: Readable says what the picture of lovers stands for.

source.text: דִּבַּ֤רְתִּי אֵלַ֨יִךְ֙ בְּשַׁלְוֺתַ֔יִךְ אָמַ֖רְתְּ לֹ֣א אֶשְׁמָ֑ע זֶ֤ה דַרְכֵּךְ֙ מִנְּעוּרַ֔יִךְ כִּ֥י לֹֽא־שָׁמַ֖עַתְּ בְּקוֹלִֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: I spoke to you in your ease; you said: Not I will listen. This [has been] your way from your youth, that not you have listened to my voice.

en.L: I spoke to you in your ease; \q you said, "I will not listen." \q This [has been] your way from your youth, \q that you have not listened to {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} voice.
en.B: I spoke to you while you felt secure, \q but you said, "I will not listen." \q Ever since you were young you have behaved like this: \q you have not obeyed {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} voice.
en.R: I warned you when life was easy for you, \q but you said, "I will not listen." \q You have acted like this ever since you were young; \q you have never obeyed {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.

decisions.choice: your ease: your times of security and prosperity
decisions.reason: The word is plural, "your times of ease": when all was well, the people saw no need to listen.

decisions.choice: from your youth: since the beginning of the nation's life
decisions.reason: Jeremiah speaks of Israel's youth as the time of the exodus and the wilderness (2:2; 3:24-25); disobedience goes back that far (7:25-26).

decisions.choice: never obeyed me
decisions.reason: To "listen to the voice" of someone means to obey them; Readable says so.

source.text: כָּל־רֹעַ֨יִךְ֙ תִּרְעֶה־ר֔וּחַ וּֽמְאַהֲבַ֖יִךְ בַּשְּׁבִ֣י יֵלֵ֑כוּ כִּ֣י אָ֤ז תֵּבֹ֨שִׁי֙ וְנִכְלַ֔מְתְּ מִכֹּ֖ל רָעָתֵֽךְ׃

records.literal_gloss: All your shepherds will shepherd [the] wind, and your lovers into captivity will go; for then you will be ashamed and humiliated because of all your evil.

en.L: The wind will shepherd all your shepherds, \q and your lovers will go into captivity; \q for then you will be ashamed and disgraced \q because of all your wickedness.
en.B: The wind will herd away all your shepherds, \q and your lovers will be carried into captivity. \q Then you will feel shame and disgrace \q because of all your wickedness.
en.R: A wind will drive all your leaders away, \q and your allies will be taken away as prisoners. \q You will be put to shame and humiliated then \q for all the evil you have done.

decisions.choice: the wind will shepherd your shepherds: the rulers will be driven off as a wind drives chaff
decisions.reason: There is a play on words: the verb "to shepherd" is from the same root as "shepherds". "Shepherds" are the kings and rulers (2:8; 23:1-4). Instead of leading the flock, they will themselves be herded away by the wind (compare 4:11-12; 13:24).

decisions.choice: then: when the leaders and allies are gone
decisions.reason: The opening word stresses what follows: only when her support is swept away will the city feel the shame of her wickedness.

decisions.choice: leaders; allies
decisions.reason: Readable says what the pictures of shepherds and lovers stand for.

source.text: יֹשַׁבְתְּ֙ בַּלְּבָנ֔וֹן מְקֻנַּ֖נְתְּ בָּֽאֲרָזִ֑ים מַה־נֵּחַנְתְּ֙ בְּבֹא־לָ֣ךְ חֲבָלִ֔ים חִ֖יל כַּיֹּלֵדָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: [You] dwelling in the Lebanon, nested in the cedars, how you will groan in [the] coming to you [of] pangs, anguish like [one] giving birth!

en.L: You who dwell in Lebanon, \q nested among the cedars, \q how you will groan when pangs come upon you, \q anguish like [a woman] giving birth!
en.B: You who live in Lebanon, \q nesting among the cedars, \q how you will groan when the pains come on you, \q pain like a woman in labor!
en.R: You live in a palace made of cedar from Lebanon, \q snug as a bird in its nest. \q But how you will groan when pain comes on you, \q pain like a woman having a baby!

decisions.choice: dwelling in Lebanon, nested in the cedars: living in Jerusalem's cedar-built palaces
decisions.reason: Jerusalem is not in Lebanon; the words describe the city's royal buildings of Lebanon cedar (verses 6-7, 14-15; 1 Kings 7:2). Like a bird nesting high in a cedar, the city feels safe.

decisions.choice: how you will groan: the verb read as a form of "groan"
decisions.reason: The form is unusual. It is probably from the verb "to groan", which suits the picture of labor pains. Others take it from the verb "to be pitied": "how you will be pitied", or, said with irony, "how pitiable you will be".

decisions.choice: you dwelling, you nested: the forms read aloud
decisions.reason: The written forms have an older ending; the forms read aloud have the usual one. Both are "you", spoken to a woman, and the meaning is the same.

decisions.choice: pangs like a woman giving birth: sudden, unavoidable anguish
decisions.reason: Jeremiah uses the pains of labor for the terror of an enemy's coming (4:31; 6:24; 13:21).

decisions.choice: in a palace made of cedar from Lebanon; snug as a bird in its nest
decisions.reason: Readable explains the picture, since the city does not lie in Lebanon.

source.text: חַי־אָנִי֮ נְאֻם־יְהוָה֒ כִּ֣י אִם־יִהְיֶ֞ה כָּנְיָ֤הוּ בֶן־יְהֽוֹיָקִים֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ יְהוּדָ֔ה חוֹתָ֖ם עַל־יַ֣ד יְמִינִ֑י כִּ֥י מִשָּׁ֖ם אֶתְּקֶֽנְךָּ׃

records.literal_gloss: [As] I live, declares Yahweh, even if were Coniah son of Jehoiakim king of Judah a signet ring on [the] hand of my right, yet from there I would tear you off.

en.L: [As] I live, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, even if Coniah son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, were a signet ring on {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} right hand, yet from there I would tear you off.
en.B: As surely as I live, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}: Coniah son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, even if you were the signet ring on {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} right hand, I would still pull you off.
en.R: As surely as I live, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}: Coniah son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, even if you were the ring with {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} seal on it, worn on {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} right hand, I would still pull you off.

decisions.choice: Coniah son of Jehoiakim: the king also called Jehoiachin and Jeconiah
decisions.reason: Jehoiakim's son reigned three months in 597 BC before he was taken to Babylon (2 Kings 24:8-15). Kings calls him Jehoiachin; Jeremiah calls him Jeconiah (24:1; 27:20) and here, and in 22:28 and 37:1, Coniah, a short form of the name. Matthew 1:11-12 calls him Jechoniah. Each verse keeps the name its Hebrew uses.

decisions.choice: a signet ring on my right hand: something precious, kept close and used to act with the owner's full authority
decisions.reason: A signet ring was engraved with its owner's seal, pressed into clay or wax to sign documents (1 Kings 21:8; Esther 8:8). Even so close and valued a king would be torn off and thrown away.

decisions.choice: the signet ring: reversed in Haggai 2:23 for Coniah's grandson
decisions.reason: After the exile God tells Zerubbabel, grandson of Jeconiah (1 Chronicles 3:17-19), "I will make you like a signet ring, for I have chosen you" (Haggai 2:23). The picture of rejection here is taken up there as a picture of restored favor to David's line.

decisions.choice: were Coniah ... I would tear you off: the speech turns from speaking about Coniah to speaking to him
decisions.reason: The sentence begins in the third person and ends in the second, as God turns to the king himself; verses 25-27 go on speaking to him.

decisions.choice: Coniah son of Jehoiakim ..., even if you were
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Coniah first and then say "you", so that the change from speaking about him to speaking to him does not confuse the reader.

source.text: וּנְתַתִּ֗יךָ בְּיַד֙ מְבַקְשֵׁ֣י נַפְשֶׁ֔ךָ וּבְיַ֛ד אֲשֶׁר־אַתָּ֥ה יָג֖וֹר מִפְּנֵיהֶ֑ם וּבְיַ֛ד נְבוּכַדְרֶאצַּ֥ר מֶֽלֶךְ־בָּבֶ֖ל וּבְיַ֥ד הַכַּשְׂדִּֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: And I will give you into [the] hand of [those] seeking your life, and into [the] hand of [those] whom you [are] fearful of their faces, and into [the] hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, and into [the] hand of the Chaldeans.

en.L: And I will give you into the hand of those who seek your life, and into the hand of those whom you dread, and into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, and into the hand of the Chaldeans.
en.B: I will hand you over to those who want to kill you, to those you fear, to Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon and to the Chaldeans.
en.R: I will hand you over to the people who want to kill you, the people you are afraid of: Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon and the Babylonians.

decisions.choice: Nebuchadrezzar: the spelling the Hebrew uses here for Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon
decisions.reason: Jeremiah mostly spells the name Nebuchadrezzar, closer to the Babylonian form; Kings and some chapters of Jeremiah spell it Nebuchadnezzar. It is the same king, who reigned 605-562 BC. Each verse keeps the form its Hebrew uses.

decisions.choice: those seeking your life: those who want to kill you
decisions.reason: To "seek someone's life" is to try to kill him (4:30; 11:21).

decisions.choice: the Chaldeans: the people of southern Babylonia whose dynasty ruled Babylon
decisions.reason: In Jeremiah the Chaldeans are the Babylonians and their army.

decisions.choice: the Babylonians (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in Isaiah, Readable says "Babylonians" for "Chaldeans".

decisions.choice: the people you are afraid of: Nebuchadrezzar ...
decisions.reason: Readable treats the last two names as saying who the feared enemies are, rather than repeating "into the hand of" four times.

source.text: וְהֵֽטַלְתִּ֣י אֹתְךָ֗ וְאֶֽת־אִמְּךָ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר יְלָדַ֔תְךָ עַ֚ל הָאָ֣רֶץ אַחֶ֔רֶת אֲשֶׁ֥ר לֹֽא־יֻלַּדְתֶּ֖ם שָׁ֑ם וְשָׁ֖ם תָּמֽוּתוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: And I will hurl you and your mother who bore you to the land another, where not you were born there, and there you will die.

en.L: And I will hurl you and your mother who bore you into another land, where you were not born, and there you will die.
en.B: I will throw you and the mother who gave birth to you into another country, where neither of you was born, and there you will both die.
en.R: I will throw you and your mother out into another country, where neither of you was born, and you will both die there.

decisions.choice: your mother: Nehushta, the queen mother, taken to Babylon with her son
decisions.reason: 2 Kings 24:8, 12, 15 names her and says she went into exile with the king in 597 BC. The queen mother held a place of honor at court (13:18; 29:2).

decisions.choice: you were born, you will die: plural, the king and his mother together
decisions.reason: The last two verbs are plural, so both are meant.

decisions.choice: hurl: throw far, as one throws a spear
decisions.reason: The verb is used for flinging something away (1 Samuel 18:11; 20:33). The same verb returns in verse 28 and in 16:13.

decisions.choice: neither of you; you will both die
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable show that the plural verbs include the king's mother.

source.text: וְעַל־הָאָ֗רֶץ אֲשֶׁר־הֵ֛ם מְנַשְּׂאִ֥ים אֶת־נַפְשָׁ֖ם לָשׁ֣וּב שָׁ֑ם שָׁ֖מָּה לֹ֥א יָשֽׁוּבוּ׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And to the land where they [are] lifting up their soul to return there, there not they will return.

en.L: But to the land to which they lift up their soul to return, there they will not return.
en.B: They will long to return to this land, but they will never come back to it.
en.R: They will long to come back home to this land, but they will never return.

decisions.choice: lift up their soul: long for, set their desire on
decisions.reason: To lift up one's soul to something is to long for it with all one's being (44:14; Deuteronomy 24:15).

decisions.choice: they: the king and his mother, and those taken with them
decisions.reason: The verse moves to "they", speaking about the exiles rather than to the king.

decisions.choice: the longing comes first (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew begins with "the land" for emphasis; Balanced and Readable begin with the longing and end with the refusal, which keeps the stress on "never".

source.text: הַעֶ֨צֶב נִבְזֶ֜ה נָפ֗וּץ הָאִ֤ישׁ הַזֶּה֙ כָּנְיָ֔הוּ אִ֨ם־כְּלִ֔י אֵ֥ין חֵ֖פֶץ בּ֑וֹ מַדּ֤וּעַ הֽוּטֲלוּ֙ ה֣וּא וְזַרְע֔וֹ וְהֻ֨שְׁלְכ֔וּ עַל־הָאָ֖רֶץ אֲשֶׁ֥ר לֹא־יָדָֽעוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: A pot despised, shattered, [is] the man this, Coniah? Or a vessel [in which] there is no pleasure in it? Why have they been hurled, he and his offspring, and been cast to the land which not they knew?

en.L: Is this man Coniah a despised, shattered pot, \q a vessel no one delights in? \q Why have they been hurled out, he and his offspring, \q and cast into a land that they did not know?
en.B: Is this man Coniah a worthless, broken pot, \q a jar that no one wants? \q Why have he and his children been hurled out \q and thrown into a land they do not know?
en.R: Is Coniah like a broken pot that people look down on, \q a jar that no one wants anymore? \q Why have he and his children been thrown out \q and sent away to a country they have never known?

decisions.choice: a pot, a vessel: a cheap clay jar, smashed and thrown out
decisions.reason: The first word is rare and seems to name a clay pot or figure; the second is the common word for a jar or dish. A cracked clay pot was simply thrown away (19:11; 48:38; Hosea 8:8).

decisions.choice: the questions: a lament that asks how the king could come to this
decisions.reason: The first questions ask whether Coniah is no more than a worthless pot; the third asks why he is cast out. They read as the people's grief and bewilderment, which verses 29-30 answer with the LORD's word.

decisions.choice: his offspring: his children and descendants
decisions.reason: Coniah was eighteen when he was exiled (2 Kings 24:8); 1 Chronicles 3:17-18 lists sons born to him, probably in Babylon. The word covers all his line, which verse 30 speaks of again.

decisions.choice: children (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "offspring"; here Balanced and Readable say "children", and in verse 30, where the line of kings is meant, "descendants".

source.text: אֶ֥רֶץ אֶ֖רֶץ אָ֑רֶץ שִׁמְעִ֖י דְּבַר־יְהוָֽה׃ס

records.literal_gloss: Land, land, land, hear [the] word of Yahweh!

en.L: Land, land, land, \q hear the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}!
en.B: Land, land, land, \q hear the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}!
en.R: Land! Land! Land! \q Listen to the message from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}!

decisions.choice: land, land, land: the threefold call makes the summons as solemn as possible
decisions.reason: Repeating a word three times gives the greatest stress (7:4; Isaiah 6:3). The land is called as a witness to the sentence that follows.

decisions.choice: land: the land of Judah, or the whole earth
decisions.reason: The word can mean a country or the earth. Since the oracle concerns Judah's king and his exile from the land, it most likely means the land of Judah; the earth may also be called to witness (6:19; Isaiah 1:2).

source.text: כֹּ֣ה׀אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֗ה כִּתְב֞וּ אֶת־הָאִ֤ישׁ הַזֶּה֙ עֲרִירִ֔י גֶּ֖בֶר לֹא־יִצְלַ֣ח בְּיָמָ֑יו כִּי֩ לֹ֨א יִצְלַ֜ח מִזַּרְע֗וֹ אִ֚ישׁ יֹשֵׁב֙ עַל־כִּסֵּ֣א דָוִ֔ד וּמֹשֵׁ֥ל ע֖וֹד בִּיהוּדָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: Thus says Yahweh: Write the man this childless, a man [who] not will prosper in his days; for not will prosper from his offspring a man sitting on [the] throne of David and ruling again in Judah.

en.L: Thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}: Write this man down [as] childless, \q a man [who] will not prosper in his days; \q for no man of his offspring will prosper, sitting on the throne of David \q and ruling again in Judah.
en.B: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} says this: Record this man as childless, \q a man who will not succeed in his lifetime, \q for none of his descendants will succeed in sitting on the throne of David \q or ruling again in Judah.
en.R: This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says: Write this man down in the records as if he had no children, \q a man who will not succeed in his lifetime. \q None of his descendants will succeed in sitting on David's throne \q or ruling in Judah again.

decisions.choice: write this man childless: list him as having no heir to the throne; none of his line will reign
decisions.reason: The picture is of a register of citizens or of a royal line (Numbers 1:18; Ezekiel 13:9). Coniah did have sons (1 Chronicles 3:17-18; verse 28 above), so "childless" does not mean he would have no children: it means that, as king, he is entered as one with no successor, because none of his descendants will sit on David's throne. No son of his ever reigned; his grandson Zerubbabel later governed Judah under Persia, but not as king (Haggai 1:1).

decisions.choice: the line of Coniah and the line of the Messiah: Matthew 1:11-12 lists Jechoniah among the ancestors of Jesus through Joseph
decisions.reason: Matthew traces the royal line from David through Jechoniah and Zerubbabel to Joseph, the husband of Mary. Christians have read this together with Jeremiah's word in several ways: that Jesus inherits the royal title through Joseph as his legal father without being Coniah's physical descendant; that Luke 3:27-31 traces another line through David's son Nathan; or that God's promise to Zerubbabel (Haggai 2:23) shows the sentence on Coniah's line was later lifted. The text of Jeremiah itself speaks of the kings of Coniah's own day and after.

decisions.choice: prosper: succeed, achieve what one sets out to do
decisions.reason: The same verb is used twice: Coniah will not succeed in his own lifetime, and none of his line will succeed in reaching the throne.

decisions.choice: in the records as if he had no children
decisions.reason: Readable explains the picture of the register and that "childless" means without an heir to the throne (see the meaning decision).

decisions.choice: Thus says the LORD: (L); The LORD says this: (B); This is what the LORD says: (R)
decisions.reason: The set wording for this formula, as in verse 3.
